t: from the altar inward. Toward the Sanctuary (Heikhal).
a revi'it. A quarter of a log (about 75 cc).
undiluted wine. Wine that is not mixed with water.
forty days have passed over it. Since it was pressed.
and interrupted it. He did not drink it continuously.
wine from the winepress within forty days. Grape juice immediately after it is pressed in the winepress, or wine that has not finished its fermentation process.
and he does not profane the service. His service is not invalid.
other intoxicants. Foods and drinks that intoxicate.
even from milk or from dried-fig cake. Since excessive consumption of them may cause a feeling of dullness (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 7:6).
to rule. To decide halakhah.
ate dates or drank milk and his mind became slightly confused. He became dazed from the large quantity of sugar.

as it is stated, "and to rule" etc.. This verse is stated at the end of the passage dealing with the prohibition of drinking wine and strong drink in the Sanctuary, and from it we learn that it is also forbidden to rule while intoxicated.
in a matter that is explicit in the Torah, until even the Sadducees know it. A law that is explicit in the Written Torah, such that even the Sadducees, who did not accept the Oral Torah, know it.
and even halakhot and midrashim. The study of halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai (law given to Moses at Sinai) and halakhic midrash on the verses.

provided that he does not rule. When he teaches Torah, even teaching that contains halakhic rulings, it is permitted if the teaching is academic in character and not halakhic, and he is not ruling halakhah for practice.
drank only a revi'it and there was in it any amount of water. So that in total he drank less than a revi'it of wine (Kesef Mishneh).
walked the distance of a mil. Walked the distance of a mil (about 900 meters).
the men of the mishmar. Priests serving in the Temple that week (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:3).
but not during the days of their Sabbath-week. During the day, throughout that entire week.
the other ancestral houses of the mishmar whose service is not today. The mishmar was divided into ancestral houses (batei avot), and each worked on one day of the week (ibid. 4:11).
the ancestral house of the day. Those serving on that day.

and knows that his ancestral houses are fixed for service today, it is forbidden for him to drink the entire day. This applies even at the time of the destruction, so that when the Temple is rebuilt he will be ready for service.
did not know his mishmar or his ancestral houses. Every day he is in doubt whether today is the day of his ancestral house.

but his remedy is his defect. His remedy (his permission to drink) stems from his defect (his not knowing which ancestral house he belongs to), for he cannot serve until it is clarified which mishmar and ancestral house he belongs to, and by then his wine will have turned sour.
a priest who let his hair grow. Who did not cut his hair for thirty days (below, halakhah 11).
and they shall not shave their heads. This is a separate prohibition against shaving all the hair of the head (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah, chapter 12).
and they shall not let their locks grow wild. They shall not grow their head hair too long.
for the priests are warned about wine only at the time of entering the Temple. Above, halakhah 1, and below, halakhah 17.
but the High Priest is forbidden to let his hair grow wild. Rather, he has his hair cut every Friday (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:6).
and to tear his garments ever. He does not tear his garments even when a relative of his dies (ibid.).
for he is always in the Temple. Ibid. 5:7.
and nazirite status is not shorter than thirty days. See also Hilchot Nezirut 3:2.
and the men of the mishmar. See above, halakhah 6.

so that they will not go up to their mishmar unkempt. Similarly, the men of the ma'amad (lay delegation) are forbidden to cut their hair and launder clothes during the week of their ma'amad (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 6:11).
one whose mishmar ended during the Festival. A priest who finished his week of service in the middle of the Festival.

he is permitted to shave during the Festival. Although the Sages forbade cutting hair and laundering on the Festival so that people would not enter the Festival unkempt, they permitted the priests of the mishmar to cut hair and launder because it had been forbidden to them to do so before the Festival (and they likewise permitted others who had no opportunity to cut hair and launder before the Festival; see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:17-19).
in the way that one tears for the dead. A tear a handbreadth long (Hilchot Evel 8:2).

and the law of one who enters like this from the altar inward and the law of one who leaves from there is the same. This prohibition does not apply only when he entered drunk, or with his hair unkempt, or with torn garments, but also if he drank inside the Temple before leaving.
even though he is not under a warning. It is not a prohibition of a negative commandment (lav).
for this is not honor and reverence for the great and holy House. It is forbidden under the law of reverence and honor for the Temple (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:1).
an Israelite who let his hair grow until it became a plait. Hair braided in an orderly manner.
except from Yom Kippur to Yom Kippur. See also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:22.

and an ordinary priest enters the Holy every day for the service. For offering the incense and lighting the lamps; on the Sabbath he also enters to arrange the showbread; and priests also enter to prostrate themselves.
or to prostrate himself. Since prostration has the status of service, and the priests would enter the Sanctuary every day to prostrate themselves there (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 6:5).

do not leave the service and go out in haste and rush because of this decree. This was said to Aaron and his sons, that they should not interrupt the service because of the death decreed upon Nadav and Avihu, and from here the prohibition is learned for all generations.
was changed. A special warning was written, since he is included among the priests.
a dead person for whom he is obligated to mourn. First-degree relatives, as detailed in Hilchot Evel 2:1-2.

even though he does not leave the Temple, he does not serve. An onen is forbidden to serve and therefore must stop the service he is engaged in, yet he is nevertheless forbidden to leave until the service is completed by another (Kesef Mishneh).
an onen by Torah law. Explained below, halakhah 9.

and he shall not go out of the Temple etc.. This refers to when he heard that someone close to him died, as emerges from the preceding verse, which speaks of his being forbidden to become impure for relatives who died.

and had I eaten the sin-offering today, would it have been good etc.. Aaron the priest explained why he did not eat the sin-offering goat when he was an onen over the death of his sons Nadav and Avihu.
and likewise he does not take a share to eat in the evening. Since he was not fit to eat the meat of the offering at the time of its offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:19-20).
an onen who served is not flogged. Since this law is not explicit in the Torah but is learned by an a fortiori argument (Kesef Mishneh, Rikevo).

and he is permitted to touch sacred items even though he has not immersed etc.. An onen, once his onenut has ended, must immerse and only then may he eat of the sacred items. This enactment is a stringency (ma'alah) that the Sages instituted regarding eating sacred items (out of concern that he was not careful about impurity while he was forbidden to eat), but regarding touching sacred items an onen is considered pure even before his immersion (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 12:15).

and likewise the day of burial, and he does not take hold of its night. On the day of burial he is considered an onen by rabbinic law, but on the night after it he is not an onen at all, not even by rabbinic law.
and the day of a recent report. When he heard of the death of one of his relatives within thirty days of the death (Hilchot Evel 7:1).
and the day of gathering the bones. The day on which the bones of one of his parents were transferred from a temporary grave to a permanent grave.
it is like the day of burial. After the day of death and on the night that follows, there is no onenut at all.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:9.
the mourner. One whose relative died, within the week after the burial.
does not send his offerings. He may not send offerings that he has pledged or is obligated to bring, even through others.
even wine or wood or frankincense. Which can be pledged and offered on their own (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1).
as long as he is not fit to enter the camp. While he is a leper, until he immerses at the end of his purification process (Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 11:1).

but the one under ban etc.. A person who transgressed a prohibition whose punishment is the ban (for the list of the prohibitions see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14) and the court placed him under the ban (for the details of the conduct of the ban see ibid. 7:4).

therefore, if they offered on his behalf, it is accepted. Initially he should not send his offerings, out of doubt, but if he sent them, the offering offered during his ban counts as his offering, and he need not bring another.
one impure through a creeping creature or the like. One who touched a dead creeping creature, as well as other impure people who immerse and become pure on the day of their impurity.
and the uncircumcised. One who has not been circumcised.
except for the Pesach-offering, which is not slaughtered etc.. Hilchot Korban Pesach 2:5.

the camp of the Shekhinah, which is from the entrance of the Israelites' courtyard inward. In the wilderness there were three camps, one inside the other: the camp of Israel, the camp of Levi, and the camp of the Shekhinah. The areas corresponding to them for all generations are: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount, and the Temple from the entrance of the courtyard inward (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:11).
he shall dwell alone; outside the camp shall be his dwelling. The leper must be alone, separated from human company, and therefore goes outside the camp of Israel.
a leper, whose impurity is severe. As explained shortly.

so too whoever's impurity is more severe, his banishment is more severe than that of his fellow. From here the Sages learned that the degree of distancing from the Temple is determined by the severity of the impurity. In addition, the Sages enacted further distancings from other areas of the Temple according to their degree of sanctity, as detailed below (see also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:13-22).
because he defiles by entering. Everything in the house becomes impure if he enters it (Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 10:12).
zavim. A man who has a pus-like discharge (similar in appearance to semen) as a result of illness (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 2:1).
and zavot. A woman who sees blood at a time other than the proper time of her menstruation (Hilchot Issurei Biah 6:2-3).

for they defile the couch and the seat even from beneath the stone. If one of these impure persons was on a vessel made for sitting or lying, even without touching the vessel and even if a stone (which does not become impure) intervened between him and the vessel, the vessel becomes impure (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 6:5). This is in contrast to corpse impurity (Hilchot Tumat Met 5:14).
what a corpse does not defile. And therefore he is banished only from the camp of the Shekhinah.
with him in the camp of Levi. The place where Moses resided in the wilderness.
the Chel. A wall ten cubits high outside the wall of the courtyard (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:3).
and those who had relations with a niddah. Impure for seven days like a niddah, but their impurity is lighter (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 3:1-2).
a tevul yom. One who has immersed; as long as the sun has not set on him he has a light impurity and is forbidden to eat terumah and sacred items (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:1-2).
the Women's Courtyard. An area east of the Israelites' courtyard (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:7).

one lacking atonement. A zav, zavah, woman after childbirth, or leper who has become pure of their impurity and has not yet brought the offering that completes their purification process; they are forbidden to eat sacred items (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
the sun has set on him. The sun has set on him, and therefore his impurity is lighter.
and the prohibition of a tevul yom in the camp of Levi. That is, in the Women's Courtyard, which is in the camp of Levi.

by rabbinic law. Likewise those forbidden to enter the Chel are so by rabbinic law (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 1:8), since the Chel and the Women's Courtyard are additional stringencies in the Temple (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:11).

and the priest shall atone for her and she shall be pure. This is said of a woman after childbirth, that only after she has brought her offerings is she fully pure; the same law applies to others lacking atonement (below 4:4).
to the other walled cities. For their definition see Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 12:15.
a leper who entered the Temple Mount is flogged eighty. He is flogged twice for two transgressions: for entering Jerusalem and for entering the Temple Mount.
makkat mardut. Flogging by rabbinic law (for rebelliousness).
a sliding-scale offering. A sin-offering whose type varies according to the person's financial means (Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).
or a person who touches any impure thing. This verse is part of the list of sins for which one who transgresses unintentionally brings a sliding-scale offering (see Leviticus 5:1-13).

an addition to the courtyard that was fully sanctified as we have explained. That it is possible to add to the area of the courtyard. For the addition to be fully sanctified, it must be done in a specific order as detailed in Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:10-14.

in corpse impurities for which the nazirite shaves. A nazirite who became impure through a corpse has his nazirite days cancelled and must shave his hair and bring offerings (Hilchot Nezirut 6:3). But this applies only if he became impure through a corpse in certain ways, for in some cases, although he is impure with seven-day impurity, his nazirite status is not cancelled (see ibid. 7:1-8).
as has already been explained regarding nezirut. Ibid. 7:2.

for he is secondary to the first one who touched a corpse. The person or vessel that became impure through a corpse is the "first who touched a corpse" (and is impure with seven-day impurity), while one who touches it is secondary (and is impure until evening).

or became impure through other primary sources of impurity of the Torah. For example, he became impure through an animal carcass or a creeping creature and the like (for the list of the primary sources of impurity from the Torah see Maimonides' Introduction to Seder Tohorot).
anyone who requires immersion in water by Torah law. One who must immerse by Torah law (one impure through a corpse, and a first-degree impure; Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 11:4).
that his sun set. That the sun set on him at the end of the day of his immersion.

even though he is a first-degree impure regarding terumah etc.. Although this person or vessel is considered a "first" (as one who touches a primary source of impurity is called; Hilchot Tumat Met 5:8), and defiles terumah and the meat of offerings, nevertheless they are exempt for entering the Temple (see also ibid. 5:5).
for these matters are a halakhah transmitted by tradition. They were received in the halakhic tradition and are not from the Torah (see ibid.).
and the like. One of the primary sources of impurity.
even if they were vessels that touched a corpse. Whose impurity is as severe as the impurity of the corpse itself.
by tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
for washing his body he is punishable by karet. As stated in the continuation of the verse: "but he shall not bathe his flesh, and he shall bear his iniquity" (above, halakhah 12).
for washing his garments he is flogged forty. For entering with impure garments that were not purified he is not liable to karet but to flogging.
as will be explained. Hilchot Tumat Met 5:2.
but a garment that is a first-degree. That one of the primary sources of impurity touched.
who inserted his hands. And did not insert his whole body.

from the primary sources of impurity of their words. For example, one who became impure from gentiles (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 2:10; for the list of the primary sources of impurity by rabbinic law see Maimonides' Introduction to Seder Tohorot).
or who ate impure foods etc.. Who by rabbinic law became impure because of them (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:10).
exempt. Provided that he did not remain inside, as explained below, halakhah 22 (Rikevo, Melekhet Shlomo).
in the manner of entering the Torah made liable. In the usual way in which people enter.
even if he entered in a tower flying in the air. A chest suspended in the air, not in the usual manner on the ground of the Temple.
any place where one is liable to karet for deliberate entry etc.. Inside the Israelites' courtyard (above, halakhah 12).
they invert a vessel over it. The pesachter (a large vessel holding a lethech; Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:13; see also ibid. 3:6).
until after the Sabbath. Since it is forbidden to move it on the Sabbath (see Hilchot Shabbat 25:6).
with plain wooden vessels. Wooden vessels with no receptacle, which cannot become impure (Hilchot Kelim 1:10).
so as not to increase the impurity. For if the vessel became impure there would be additional impurity in the Temple.
to a pure Temple. In which there was no impurity.
for there was a corpse under a tent in the Temple. And therefore anyone who enters under that tent becomes impure through the corpse.

for his entry and his impurity come together. Although before he entered the Temple he was pure, since he became impure immediately upon entering he is considered as entering while impure, and not as one who was pure and became impure in the Temple, whose law is explained shortly.
prostrated himself on his way out toward the outside is exempt. For this does not have the status of prostration but of ordinary remaining.
long enough to read etc.. The time it takes to recite the verse at an average pace (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 2:3).
and this is the measure of prostration. This is the time that prostration usually takes.
even though he did not remain. For if he remained he is liable to karet even if he did not serve (above 3:22).
and they will die through it when they profane it. Regarding a non-priest who ate terumah (Hilchot Terumot 6:6).
and any negative commandment for which one is liable to death at the hands of Heaven, one is flogged for it. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1.
his brothers the priests etc.. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:6.

and how is it possible for him to serve and not remain until he becomes liable to karet. For the measure of time an impure person remains before becoming liable to karet is extremely short (see above 3:23).
and he leaves by the shortest way. He leaves by the shortest route, for otherwise he is liable to karet even if he did not remain (ibid. halakhah 22).
the tzinor. A kind of fork with which the limbs of the offerings are turned over.
for anything that brings one close to the service is like the service. See also below 9:4.
before his sun set. Before the sun sets; then he is called a tevul yom.
by tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
for he is still impure. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:1-2.
one lacking atonement. For its explanation see above 3:6.
and the priest shall atone for her and she shall be pure. See the explanation above 3:7.
if it is a known impurity. That people were aware of this impurity before this person became impure.
and if it is the impurity of the abyss. Corpse impurity that was never known to anyone before the priest became impure.
the tzitz atones. The tzitz (High Priest's forehead plate) causes this offering, which should have been invalid and profaned, to be an accepted offering.
even though he is deliberate. Who knows that he is impure at the time he throws the blood.
and we have already explained the impurity of the abyss regarding nezirut. Hilchot Nezirut 6:18-19.
the things that are offered. The parts of the offerings that are offered on the altar.
the impurity of the edible parts. The meat of the offering that is eaten.
the impurity that is pushed aside for the community. Below, halakhah 9.
on his forehead. Of the High Priest.
and tomorrow, tomorrow. And even if it is not offered tomorrow it will be offered the day after.
and every offering that has a fixed time. That there is a defined time at which it must be offered.
whether an individual's offering. For example the Pesach-offering.
overrides the Sabbath. It is offered on the Sabbath.

all the community offerings have a fixed time. Except for the bull for a communal unwitting ruling and the communal idolatry goat, which although they are community offerings have no fixed time (Rikevo).
is burned like other sacred items that became impure. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashim 19:1.

and most of the congregation who offer it were impure through a corpse. It is forbidden to offer the offering of one impure through a corpse (above 2:12), but when most of the congregation is impure, although the congregation is the owner of the community offerings, the prohibition of offering for the impure is set aside (according to Or Sameach).
the service vessels are impure through a corpse. And offerings cannot be offered without those service vessels.
and the impure and the pure attend to it together. Since the offering comes in impurity, they are not particular that only the pure attend to it.
are liable to karet for entry. According to the law of impure persons who entered the courtyard (above 3:12).

even though they were permitted only into the courtyard. For offering the Pesach-offering one must enter the courtyard to slaughter the Pesach-offering there and throw the blood on the altar, and there is no need to enter the Sanctuary.
since I do not read of them "outside the camp you shall send them". For they are permitted to enter the courtyard.
ancestral house. The priests who must serve in the Temple on that day (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:11).

even though most of them are impure through a corpse, only the pure shall offer. Although most of the priests of the ancestral house are impure (or even if all are), impurity is not permitted, since there are other priests who can serve.
let another ancestral house come. From the mishmar of priests of that week.
the mishmar. Each week a different mishmar served in the Temple that week (ibid. 4:3).

if most of the priests present there in Jerusalem etc.. When no pure priests of the mishmar are found, and most of the priests in Jerusalem are impure, this situation is regarded as impurity in the community, and the impurity is set aside. In this situation both the impure and the pure serve together (as described above, halakhah 12).
at the fixed time. For offering the offering.
and there were men who were impure through a human corpse. These people were forbidden to offer the Pesach-offering, and they made the Second Pesach.
by tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
and the matter is explicit in the Writings etc.. That when most of the community was impure they offered the Pesach-offering in impurity, as was done in the first year of Hezekiah's reign.
not as it is written. This implies that the matter was not done properly.

because he intercalated that year because of the impurity. In that year there was no reason to intercalate the year and add an extra month, yet Hezekiah ruled to intercalate the year because most of the congregation was impure and would not have had time to purify before Pesach unless the year were intercalated (although in the end, despite the intercalation, most of the congregation did not manage to purify).
and we have already explained in Kiddush HaChodesh. Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 4:6.
and there was another one there. Another fault occurred in the intercalation of that year.

that King Hezekiah intercalated etc.. The decision to intercalate the year must be made by the 29th of Adar; after that, even though the month of Nisan has not yet been sanctified, the year may not be intercalated.
as we have explained in Kiddush HaChodesh. 4:14.
that their offering was accepted. They fulfilled the obligation of the Pesach-offering although the intercalation of the year was not done properly.
from it. From the laver.
in the morning. In the morning before he begins to serve, and likewise every hour before he begins to serve (Me'iri-Kesef Mishneh).
as it is stated. In the passage of the laver and the commandment of washing.
as we have explained. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:4.
urinates. Urinates.
and does not divert his attention. Rather, he must keep his hands in mind, knowing that they are sanctified for service.

his hands became impure. For example, he touched with his hands a person who was a first-degree impure or impure foods and drinks, so that his body is pure but his hands became impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 8:1), and to touch sacred items he must immerse them (ibid. 12:12).
and he does not need to return and sanctify. For sanctification of the hands and feet is not a matter of impurity and purity.

his body became impure through eating impure foods etc.. This impurity is rabbinic, and therefore after it the one who immerses is pure and can serve immediately, and does not need to wait for sunset (ibid. 9:1; but one who requires sunset presumably diverts his attention. In any case, if he became impure close to the end of the day and did not divert his attention and did not sanctify his hands after the immersion, his service is valid - Bavli, Zevachim 20b).

a High Priest who did not immerse and did not sanctify his hands and feet etc.. On Yom Kippur the High Priest performs some of the day's services in his eight regular garments, and some in special Yom Kippur garments. When he changes garments between services he must immerse and sanctify his hands and feet before the immersion and after it (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 2:1-2).
they are not equal for Aaron and his sons. The laws of these immersions and sanctifications are special to the High Priest and do not apply to ordinary priests.
for this is the first sanctification. At the beginning of the morning service.
the laver. A vessel designated for this purpose (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:18).
of the service vessels. Vessels sanctified for the Temple service.
outside. Outside the courtyard.
and one does not sanctify inside the laver or inside a service vessel. In a way that he puts his hands and feet into them.
but from them. The water must be poured from the vessel over the hands and feet.
and if he sanctified inside it and served, he did not profane. But if he wants to serve, he must sanctify again.
in the waters of a mikveh. Which purify the impure.
even in a spring. One who purifies in ways in which a mikveh does not purify.
whether they contain a revi'it or do not contain a revi'it. Unlike the vessel required for washing the hands for a meal, which must contain a revi'it (Hilchot Berakhot 6:12).
living water. Spring water.
rather they must be like water fit for immersion. See Hilchot Mikva'ot 7:1.
mud that is spat etc.. Thin mud like spittle (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 7:1), which is fit for an animal to drink.
completes the water of the laver. Completes the amount of water that must be in the laver (below, halakhah 13).
anything that completes the waters of a mikveh. For details see Hilchot Mikva'ot 7:3.
there is no less than enough to sanctify from it four priests. Not less than the amount needed to sanctify the hands and feet of four priests.
as it is stated. Regarding washing from the laver.

are disqualified through remaining overnight. They are disqualified for sanctifying from them if they remained overnight in the laver, like every service vessel, which disqualifies what is in it through remaining overnight.
as we have explained. Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:18.

they sink it in the waters of a mikveh etc.. At night they would lower the laver into a mikveh or spring and connect the water in it to those waters, thus preventing the water from being disqualified by remaining overnight.

or fill it every day in the morning. Alternatively one can empty the laver at night and fill it with fresh water in the morning. In the Second Temple there was a special device (a "mechonah") from which they filled the laver with fresh water every morning (ibid.).

the Sea that Solomon made. A large round copper basin that King Solomon built in the First Temple (see I Kings 7:23-26). A water channel from the spring of Ein Etam ran through it, and therefore the water in it was not disqualified by remaining overnight (although it was a service vessel), and it could be used to fill the laver each morning.
and bends down. Bends over.
and anything that interposes in immersion. For the list of things that interpose in immersion see Hilchot Mikva'ot, chapter 2.

because his warning is from a general positive commandment. A prohibition not stated in the Torah in negative language but derived from the wording of a positive commandment is not considered a negative commandment but a positive commandment.
standing on the floor. Barefoot.
disqualified. His service.
and likewise if there was an interposition between his hand and the vessel with which he serves, he disqualified. See also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:9.
anything such that if the vessel or stone were removed he could stand on one foot. Then he is not relying in his standing on the vessel or stone but on the floor.
received. The blood, an act that is considered a service of the offerings.
in the right, and the left assists. The left hand only helped the receiving that was done by the right hand, and the service was not performed with it.
for no attention is paid to one who assists. Assisting is not considered an act.
one of the stones of the courtyard shook etc.. Compare Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 1:10.
blemish. An external defect in the body (below, halakhah 7).
a permanent blemish... a passing blemish. See below, halakhah 4.
from the altar inward. From the start of the place of the altar westward (Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 69).
by tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
a broken leg or a broken hand. This refers to where the break is visible externally; see below 7:9.

garav or yalefet, which is chazazit. Yalefet is called chazazit in the vernacular. Garav and yalefet are kinds of skin eruptions, and each has two types: one that is a permanent blemish (below 7:10), and another that is a passing blemish (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:7).

blemishes that disqualify the priest from serving and the animal from being offered. For there is also a prohibition against consecrating and offering an animal that has a blemish (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:1-5; these blemishes are detailed below in chapter 7, and in Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach chapter 2 additional blemishes are listed that exist only in animals).
blemishes that disqualify only a person from serving. Below, chapter 8.
blemishes that do not disqualify but only because of appearances etc.. Below 8:17.

for example, one whose kidney was removed, or his spleen. These are examples of blemishes because of which the person or animal is not considered a treifah (Arukh HaShulchan 44:12, R. Y. Kafih; and see Hilchot Shechitah 8:25, 6:20).

whose intestines were perforated... who became a treifah. The same applies to an animal (ibid. 6:13), but when an animal becomes a treifah it may not be offered as an offering (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:10).
treifah. An animal or person inclined to die because of a defect, wound, or the like.
the uncircumcised. A person who has not been circumcised.
like a foreigner. Like a gentile.
he profaned his service and is flogged like a non-priest who served. Below 9:1.
but he is not liable to death. Although a non-priest who served is liable to death (ibid.).
a priest who was marrying women in transgression. Who married women forbidden to him.
that the court make him vow. That he vow to derive no benefit from the woman forbidden to him.
on the opinion of the many, so that he will have no annulment. For one who vows on the opinion of the many, his vow is not released except for the sake of a mitzvah (Hilchot Shevuot 6:8).
and he serves, and goes down, and divorces. After the vow he may serve immediately, and after he finishes his service he goes and divorces his wife.

until he accepts upon himself in court that he will not become impure. He does not need to vow. And since one who marries women in transgression has a strong inclination to continue his conduct, he must vow, and accepting it upon himself in court is not enough (Bavli, Bekhorot 45b).

challal. One born from a forbidden union of a priest with a woman forbidden to him because of his priesthood (Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:1-5); a challal is not considered a priest and has the law of an Israelite in every respect (ibid. 19:10).
the Great Court sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone. Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17.

and they examine the priests for lineage. That they belong to the family of priests and are not challalim; after their examination the priest does not need a further examination (Hilchot Issurei Biah 20:2).
sits in the Wood Chamber. One of the chambers of the Women's Courtyard (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:8).
removes worms from the wood for the pyre. Removes worms from the wood, for any wood in which a worm is found is invalid for the pyre (ibid.).
and he takes a share of the sacred items etc.. He receives a portion of the meat of the sacred items like his unblemished brothers.
the men of his ancestral house. Those serving in the Temple on that day (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:11).

all the blemishes that disqualify both a person and an animal. The next chapter lists the blemishes that disqualify only a person, while Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach chapter 2 lists additional blemishes special to animals.
the cartilage of his ear. The elastic cartilage of which the outer ear is built, which is the thick, harder part of the ear and is not truly soft skin.
so that the fingernail catches on the notch. That if he runs a fingernail along its back, it catches on the notch.
but the skin surrounding the cartilage of the ear. The soft flesh around the ear.
like a karshinah. A grain of the karshinah, a kind of legume called bitter vetch (Vicia ervilia), whose diameter is 3.5-5.5 mm.
even a kid, whose ears are naturally drooping and folded. Because they are exceptionally long.
the baris of the eye. The eyelid (the skin covering the eye, not the hair on it).
the charutz mentioned in the Torah. See also below, halakhah 11.
the blind one. Whose eyes (or one eye) were uprooted or are visibly not seeing externally.
because water descended permanently opposite his pupils. A kind of inflammation that seriously impairs vision.

because there were permanent sanverim in it. Permanent loss or blurring of vision that is not visible externally. If the water or the sanverim are not permanent, they are considered a passing blemish (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:7; the method of checking whether they are permanent is explained there 2:12-16).
like a grape. A protrusion in the eye resulting from inflammation of the cornea.
one in whose eye extra flesh emerged etc.. Extra flesh extended over the eye.
for there are no blemishes in the white. Defects in the white of the eye are not to be counted as a blemish.
that it be floating above the black. That the white spot protrudes above the black part.
in the nose. In the nose.
one whose nose was pierced. In one of the outer walls of the nose (a hole in the septum disqualifies only an animal; see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:2).

provided that it splits from its outer part. That the split is in the outer, protruding part of the lip (and not the inside of the mouth), and its defect is visible externally (Radbaz; Arukh HaShulchan 46:11 explains that the split is at the edge of the lip that touches the other lip).
one whose lower jaw bone exceeds the upper. The lower jaw protrudes outward more than the upper.
balum. Swollen (a second explanation is in Rashi, Bekhorot 40b, and according to Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 309, this is Maimonides' opinion).
because of his body and his creation. That he was born this way.
because of the wind. Because of illness.
most of the speaking part of his tongue. Most of the part of the tongue that is not attached to the palate.
the gid. The male organ.
was crushed. Was pounded into small pieces.
was severed. The organ was cut but some connection still remains.
or was cut off. Cut off entirely.
the testicles. The testes.
were severed. The testicles from the cords connecting them, but some connection still remains.

were cut off. The testicles were cut off entirely from the sinews that connect them, even if they lie in the scrotum (Bavli, Bekhorot 39b; from Rashi it also appears that severing is by hand and cutting off is by knife).

one who has only one testicle even though he has two sacs. For the scrotum and the testes form in separate processes. This refers to a case where one of his testicles remained inside the body during its formation and did not descend into the scrotum (see also Hilchot Bekhorot 3:5).
the tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered over, so it is not evident whether he is male or female. [Note: in the Commentary on the Mishnah, Maimonides vocalizes this word: tumtom.]
the androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.
the limper. The lame.
one whose thigh was dislocated. Whose thigh bone came out of its place and whose leg appears dislocated.
provided that it is noticeable. That it is visible externally.
one whose legs are balumot etc.. Who cannot spread his legs properly or whose legs are swollen (see above, halakhah 7, regarding a balum mouth).
dry garav. A kind of dry skin eruption.
any amount. Even a very small amount.

Egyptian chazazit. A kind of eruption dry on the outside and moist on the inside (Bavli, Bekhorot 41a; see Tosafot there and Rashi on Deuteronomy 28:27, who explained that the chazazit is moist outside and dry inside).
in which a slit was made. In which a slit was made.
the ribs. The ribs.
but the treifah is valid in a person. Above 6:7.
and invalid in an animal. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:10.
one born by caesarean. Who was not born through the womb but by caesarean section.
and invalid in an animal. Ibid. 3:4.
the mezohan. Foul-smelling.
washes and rubs his whole body with perfume. So that during service he will not be foul-smelling.
all the blemishes special to a person. One who serves with these blemishes is flogged, but his service is valid and not profaned (above 6:6).
one whose forehead protrudes toward his face like a hammer. His forehead protrudes forward, like a mallet.
a row. A line.
until he appears as though slumped between his shoulders. His neck is long and his head seems to droop.
dangling downward. Because of their great length.
in the eyebrows. The eyebrows.
whose eyebrows lie down. Over his eyelids, because of their length (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 7:2).
one who has only one eyebrow. Whose two eyebrows are joined.
one who has more than two eyebrows. Each of whose eyebrows is divided into several eyebrows (Chazon Ish, Bekhorot 26:5).
the baris of the eye. In the eyelid.
who has no hair at all on the eyelids. But if he had hair and it fell out, he is disqualified only because of appearances (below, halakhah 17).
abundant and thick. That the eyelash hair is very abundant and tangled together (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 7:3).
one that is sparse. Thin.
close to his forehead. Next to the forehead.
and they do not extend slightly lengthwise. They do not have a slightly elliptical shape.
whose tears flow constantly. His eyes tear all the time.
one with moisture flowing from the head of his eye... or from the tail of his eye. A constant discharge comes out of the eye from the end of the eye near the nose or near the temples.
one whose eyesight is mixed up. Cross-eyed.
and one is peituchah. Having a mixed tint of two colors.
whose nose ridge. The upper part of the nose.

even if he does not apply eye-paint to both his eyes at once. Even if he cannot apply eye makeup to both eyes at once because his nose protrudes slightly and obstructs the brush, he is nevertheless disqualified.
one whose middle of the nose protrudes upward. He has a bump in the middle of his nose.
whose nose tip. The lower end of his nose.
whose nose is large relative to his limbs. His nose is large relative to his other organs.
with the little finger of his hand. The pinky.
whose belly is swollen. His abdomen is swollen.

whose navel protrudes. His navel protrudes beyond the level of the surface of the belly, unlike most people, whose navel is sunken below the surface of the belly (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 7:5).
one whose breasts lie on his belly like the breasts of a woman. His chest protrudes like the breasts of a woman.
whose spine. His backbone.
from whose spine a vertebra stuck out. A vertebra slipped over other vertebrae.
and this is the one with a chatoret. The one mentioned in the Mishnah (Bekhorot 7:1).
and became like a chatoret. Hunchbacked, one with a protrusion in his back.
even if there were six and six. Even if he has an equal number of fingers on both hands.
and if there was a bone in it, even if he cut it off, he is disqualified. For then it is considered as though he lacks a limb.
joined up to below the joint. The fingers are joined together beyond the joint.
a pikah. An extra bit of flesh like a round protrusion (below, halakhah 13).
left-handed in his right hand. Left-handed.
to his knees. His knees.
that were smeared. That were crushed.
one with wind in his testicles. Whose scrotum is swollen.
one whose shins are bent so that he joins foot to foot and his knees do not touch each other. The bones of his shins are crooked and he cannot bring his knees together.
the round bone above the heel on the inside. The ankle bone protrudes more than usual.
and it resembles the spindle whorl with which women spin. Something like a half circle around which women wind the spinning thread (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 21:1).
whose sole. His foot.
even though it is not joined like that of a goose. Although his toes are not joined like the toes of a goose, it is considered a blemish.
one from whose big toe a pikah comes out. A round protrusion, an extra piece of flesh, from his big toe.
the toes of his feet are joined up to below the joint. The toes are joined together beyond the joint.
one whose entire foot is even. The width of his foot is the same in all its parts.
one whose foot is bent like a sickle. His foot is bent in the shape of a semicircle.
one who strikes with his ankles when he walks. His shins bend inward and his ankles knock against each other as he walks.
strikes with his knees when he walks. His shins bend outward and his knees knock against each other as he walks.
one who is left-handed in his right foot. Left-footed.
whose body is larger than his limbs. Proportionally.
until they are set apart from the rest of the people. The very tall and the dwarf.
red as scarlet. The skin of his flesh is red like wool dyed with the scarlet worm (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:13).

those with pure afflictions etc.. Whose skin in one place became dull and whitish, but this whiteness is fainter than an eggshell and does not make them impure (Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 1:1; those with impure leprosy are forbidden to serve because of their impurity, above 4:1).
of itself. And not through an external cause.
the scar of a burn etc.. A mark that forms in the skin at the place that heals from a burn, even if its appearance is strong, is pure (ibid. 4:3).
a shumah. A spot on the skin.
like an issar. The size of a small coin.

those with dilduli etc.. Whose skin is loose and hanging and who appear to have hollows like pockets in their skin (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 7:6; according to Rashi, pieces of flesh hang from his body).
the moisture in the skin that hung loose. Fat that separated from the body.
the deaf-mute. One who neither speaks nor hears (Hilchot Ishut 2:26).
the fool. One lacking understanding.
the epileptic etc.. One who suffers from the falling sickness (epilepsy), even if he suffers from it only rarely.
whom an evil spirit terrifies. Seized by madness as a result of an excess of black bile (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 7:5).
and these are disqualified because of appearances. If they served, their service is valid and they are not flogged (above 6:6).
whose eyelashes fell out. But if he had no hair at all in his eyelids he is entirely disqualified (above, halakhah 5).
by tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
a complete service. A full service, which completes the service and after which there is no other service.
for the throwing. Of the blood.
and for the burning. Of things that go up on the altar.
the pouring of the water on the Festival. Sukkot (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:6).
the pouring of the wine always. The wine that comes with the offering and is poured on the altar (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:1).
who threw. The blood from the vessel.
inside. On the altar in the Sanctuary.
outside. On the outer altar in the courtyard (Me'iri-Kesef Mishneh, Har HaMoriah).
who sprinkled. The blood with his finger.
any of the sprinklings of blood. This includes squeezing out and sprinkling the blood of bird offerings (Kesef Mishneh, Har HaMoriah).

any of the sprinklings in the leper's offerings. The seven sprinklings that he sprinkles in the courtyard toward the Holy of Holies from the log of oil that the leper brings, and the sprinklings he sprinkles on the leper himself from the blood of the guilt-offering and from the oil (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).
burned limbs. Of the offerings.
or a kometz. A portion of the meal-offering that is offered on the altar.
or frankincense. Brought with the meal-offering or by itself, and all of it is offered on the altar.
turned over limbs that had not been consumed. Limbs of the offerings on the altar that had not been completely burned.
once he burns a k'zayit he is liable. For this is the minimum measure of burning (see also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:2).
his two full hands. Both palms full (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 4:1).
the measure explicit in the Torah. Leviticus 16:12.
and one who arranges two logs of wood on the pyre. Every day they would place two logs on the altar's fire together with the daily offering (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:2).
for the wood is an offering. Burning the wood on the pyre is considered an offering (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1).
the one who pours. Pours oil on the meal-offerings.
and the one who mixes. Mixes the oil of the meal-offering into its fine flour.
and the one who breaks into pieces. Crumbles the meal-offering into pieces.
and the one who salts. Sprinkles salt on the meal-offering or the offering.
and the one who waves. Moves the offering or meal-offering that requires waving back and forth and up and down.
and the one who brings near. Brings the meal-offering to the corner of the altar.

and the one who arranges the showbread or the bowls of frankincense on the table. On the golden table in the Sanctuary, two rows of showbread were arranged the whole week, with two bowls of frankincense beside them (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:2).
and the one who tends the lamps. Removes the old wicks from them.
and the one who takes the handful. The handful from the meal-offering, without burning it.
and the one who receives the blood. From the offerings into a vessel.
even though he disqualified. For all of them are considered services and are included in the prohibition.
the flaying. Skinning the offerings.
and the cutting up. Cutting the limbs of the offerings.
and likewise lighting the lamps is valid by non-priests. For the lighting is not considered service (Bavli, Yoma 24b).
if the priest tended the lamps. If the priest removed the old wicks and arranged the new ones, for this is a service requiring a priest (above, halakhah 5).
and took them outside. For the menorah is in the Sanctuary, where an Israelite is forbidden to enter.
removing the ashes. Taking the remains of the offerings burned the previous evening and placing them beside the altar (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:10-12).

it must be a service of giving etc.. The verse "and the non-priest who approaches shall die" is said about a "service of giving" - a service that involves giving (burning, throwing, and pouring), and not a service whose essence is removal (removing the ashes, cleaning the altar and the menorah).
cleaned the golden altar. Removing the remains of the ashes of the golden altar from incense burned the previous evening (ibid. 3:4).
and the menorah. Removing the remains of the wicks and oil from the lamps lit the previous evening (ibid. 3:12).

arranged the pyre etc.. A non-priest who arranged and set the wood in the fires of the pyre on the top of the altar. Although he is exempt from death for this service, the wood must be arranged again by a priest.
services for which the non-priest is liable to death. Throwing, burning, and pouring (above, halakhah 2).

a tevul yom and one lacking atonement. An impure person who must bring offerings, after he immerses, is on that day a tevul yom (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:1-2), and since he has not yet brought his offerings he is also lacking atonement (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
who became impure. With an additional impurity.
and he also lacks garments and has not washed hands and feet and served. And in addition he served without garments and without sanctifying hands and feet.

is liable for each and every one. Death or flogging for each prohibition he transgressed in his service for which there is liability (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1, 19:2), and therefore he is flogged several times, having transgressed each and every prohibition several times.
and if he was a non-priest he is flogged only once. For all these prohibitions were said only regarding priests fit for service (Kesef Mishneh, Rikevo).
a non-priest who served on the Sabbath. And in his service transgressed one of the Sabbath prohibitions.
they shall not approach me to serve as priests. The verse deals with priests who served in houses of idolatry and ministered to it (see Ezekiel 44:12).
whether one who serves it in ministry. Who served before the idol with services performed by priests in the Temple.
who became a kumer. An idolatry minister.

one who slaughters for idolatry unintentionally etc.. Since he did not minister to the idolatry with services special to priests, and did so unintentionally. But if he slaughtered intentionally, his service is invalid.

one who transgressed and made a house outside the Temple to offer offerings there to the Name. Like Choni son of Shimon HaTzaddik, who went to Alexandria in Egypt and built a temple there in which offerings were offered to the name of God (see Bavli, Menachot 109b).

is not like a house of idolatry. For the service there is done for the name of God. But since there is a prohibition against offering outside the Temple, a priest who served there is disqualified from serving in the Temple.
one who serves idolatry. Above, halakhah 13.
the non-priest. Above, halakhah 1.
one with a blemish. Above 6:1.
the uncircumcised. Above 6:8.
the impure. Above 4:1.
a tevul yom. Above 4:4.
one lacking atonement. Ibid.
the onen. Above 2:7.
the drunkard. Above 1:1.
one lacking garments. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:4.
one with extra garments. Ibid. 10:4.
with torn garments. Above 1:14.
with unkempt hair. Above 1:8.
who has not washed hands and feet. Above 5:1.
the one who sits. Above 5:17.
one with an interposition between his feet and the ground. Ibid.
one with an interposition between his hand and the vessel. Ibid.
one who served with his left. Above 5:18.
